findings.section: Worked Example, Computing NPV (also Key Concepts 2, line 18)
findings.claim: The source's rule for mutually exclusive projects ... applies ...: "a 30 per cent return on $1,000 can be dominated by a 12 per cent return on $1,000,000." / IRR ignores scale; "a 30 per cent return on $1,000" can be dominated by "a 12 per cent return on $1,000,000" (Ch 16.5, ...)
findings.failure_mode: Invented quotation. The words and figures are presented as the source's (quote marks, 'the source's rule', Ch 16.5 citation) but appear nowhere in the source or deep ref. The source's own illustration is Sam's Sporting Goods' regular vs heavy-duty embroidery machine (NPV $2,835.62 at IRR 14.10% vs NPV $3,970.67 at IRR 13.20%).
findings.evidence: grep '1,000,000' in converted source: no IRR/scale example. Source 27402-27428 (Ch 16.5, Table 16.11): 'the rule is to take the project with the highest NPV'. Deep 589, 833.
findings.fix: correct: drop the quotation marks and the attribution; either label the $1,000 / $1,000,000 contrast as an illustration, or use the source's own case: the heavy-duty machine (IRR 13.20%, NPV $3,970.67) beats the regular machine (IRR 14.10%, NPV $2,835.62) because 'the rule is to take the project with the highest NPV' [V] (Ch 16.5).

findings.claim: This is the most common mis-ranking in engineering portfolios.
findings.failure_mode: Empirical frequency claim with no basis in the source or deep ref (the source has no engineering-portfolio data).
findings.evidence: Deep 573-589 (Ch 16.3, 16.5): IRR's scale problem stated as a method flaw; no frequency data.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: The five capital-budgeting methods and their software-relevant disadvantages.
findings.failure_mode: Count: Ch 16 presents six methods; the entry lists the five other than NPV (covered in Key Concept 1) but labels them as the full set.
findings.evidence: Deep 559-585: payback, NPV, IRR, PI, discounted payback, MIRR.
findings.fix: correct: **The other five capital-budgeting methods and their software-relevant disadvantages.**

findings.claim: For software firms with low debt and high equity costs, WACC is often dominated by the cost of equity (CAPM-derived), which means even modest project-specific risk increments push the appropriate discount rate substantially higher. / Software firms typically sit on the low-debt side because their assets are intangible, their cash flows are volatile, and their distress costs (loss of engineering talent, customer churn) are high.
findings.failure_mode: Software-industry capital-structure facts and causes the source does not give (Table 17.7 has no software row), plus a non sequitur: equity's share of WACC does not make a project-risk increment larger.
findings.evidence: Source 29175-29221 (Table 17.7): no software row; nearest proxies Retail (online) 6.67% debt, Computers/peripherals 8.55% debt. Deep 643: 'Firms with higher costs of financial distress have lower optimal leverage'; indirect distress costs = loss of customers and suppliers.
findings.fix: correct: line 24 → 'Table 17.7 has no software row, but the nearest proxies (online retail 6.67 per cent debt, computers/peripherals 8.55 per cent) sit at the low-debt end; trade-off theory says firms with higher distress costs carry less debt (Ch 17.5).' Line 22: strip the 'which means ...' clause.

findings.claim: For software businesses where deferred-revenue accounting can produce profitable-looking statements with poor cash conversion, this distinction is load-bearing
findings.failure_mode: Not in the source, and inverted for the usual case: deferred (unearned) revenue arises when cash arrives before revenue is recognised, which makes cash conversion look better than earnings, not worse.
findings.evidence: Deep 167-191 (Ch 4 accrual accounting) and 226 (Ch 5.5 earnings-quality test) carry no deferred-revenue claim. Source 7924: unearned revenue is money received for product not yet shipped (a current liability).
findings.fix: correct: For software businesses, the text's earnings-quality test applies directly: 'a firm reporting a strong profit but very little cash flow might raise some questions as to what was recorded to drive profits that isn't also driving cash flows' [V] (Ch 5.5).

findings.claim: The book takes a position that the payables-deferral period "probably cannot be optimised without violating credit terms" / "there can be tremendous pressure on management to perform . . . Ethical behavior is crucial in this area" (Ch 18.1)
findings.failure_mode: Quotations copied from the deep ref's [V] passages without the [V] marker; line 28 also alters the source spelling ('optimised' for 'optimized').
findings.evidence: Source 31599: 'probably cannot be optimized without violating credit'. Source 29895-29901 (Ch 18.1). Deep 659 carries the Ch 18.1 passage as [V].
findings.fix: re-mark: [V] on both; restore 'optimized' at line 28.

findings.claim: Taking the discount is often the highest-return short-term financial decision available. / (often 30+ per cent annualised) / Often 30+ per cent annualised cost when discounts are forgone
findings.failure_mode: Generalises one worked example (2/10 net 30 = 36.73 per cent) into a frequency claim and a 'highest-return' ranking the source does not make.
findings.evidence: Deep 705 (Ch 19.2): 2/10 net 30 forgone costs 36.73 per cent, 'far more than most firms pay for short-term financing'. Deep 837: 'can be 36+ per cent annualised'.
findings.fix: correct: line 30 → 'Forgoing the discount on 2/10 net 30 terms costs more than most firms pay for short-term financing (Ch 19.2).' Lines 121, 168: 'on 2/10 net 30 terms, 36.73 per cent annualised'.

findings.claim: For software-business decisions, beta estimates often disagree across sources by more than a factor of two (Ch 17.3, Table 17.3) / Beta estimates for software firms vary widely across sources (the text flags this at Table 17.3)
findings.failure_mode: Misapplied to software. The text's factor-of-two example is Goodyear's equity-cost range (9.20 to 21.08 per cent); the one software firm in Table 17.3, Microsoft, has betas of 1.19 vs 0.79. Only one of eight betas (Kroger 0.31 vs 0.66) differs by more than a factor of two, so 'often' also overstates.
findings.evidence: Deep 618 ('for some firms ... equity cost of capital ... differ by more than a factor of two'). Source 28680-28720 (Table 17.3 rows; Goodyear discussion; 'one estimate is more than twice as large as another').
findings.fix: correct: Equity-cost estimates for the same firm can differ widely across data sources — for Goodyear, 9.20 to 21.08 per cent (Ch 17.3, Table 17.3) — so treat WACC as a range, not a point estimate.

findings.claim: Mitigations are stock-based compensation, performance-tied incentives, and transparent reporting.
findings.failure_mode: 'Transparent reporting' is not among the source's mitigations; penalties and the hostile-takeover threat are dropped.
findings.evidence: Deep 102 (Ch 2.4, 'How to Resolve Agency Problems'): incentives for performance and ethical behaviour; stock-based compensation; penalties for poor performance, shortsightedness, unethical behaviour; hostile takeover threat. Source 3553-3590.
findings.fix: correct: Mitigations are performance and ethics incentives, stock-based compensation that rewards long-term thinking, penalties for poor or unethical performance, and the discipline of a takeover threat (Ch 2.4).

findings.claim: misaligned incentives in fixed-price contracts produce the classic moral-hazard pattern / What is the moral-hazard risk in fixed-price contracts? ... (Ch 2.4) / Agency theory for contractor moral-hazard (Ch 2.4)
findings.failure_mode: 'Moral hazard' is not in the source; citing it to Ch 2.4 attaches an outside concept to the section. Ch 2.4's agency problem (agent furthering personal goals at the principal's expense) supports the extension to vendors and contractors, if labelled as the distillation's.
findings.evidence: grep 'moral hazard' in converted source: no hits. Deep 96-100 (Ch 2.4 agency problems: stockholders vs management, investors vs creditors, stockholders vs other stakeholders).
findings.fix: correct: replace 'moral hazard' with 'agency problem' and mark the vendor/contractor application as an extension of Ch 2.4's principal-agent frame, not a case the text treats.

findings.claim: Excel's NPV function "assumes the first cash flow occurs one period in the future" ... Software-business practitioners who build their own capital-budgeting spreadsheets without knowing this routinely undercount the upfront investment by one period of discount.
findings.failure_mode: The quoted phrase is the deep ref's paraphrase, not source wording; 'routinely' is an unsupported frequency claim.
findings.evidence: Deep 341 (paraphrase, no marker). Source 27766-27773 (Ch 16.6): 'you must remember to include references only to the cells that contain cash flows from year 1 to the end of the project. Then, subtract the initial investment of year 0'.
findings.fix: correct: Excel's NPV function treats the first cash flow in its range as one period away, so 'include references only to the cells that contain cash flows from year 1 to the end of the project. Then, subtract the initial investment of year 0' [V] (Ch 16.6). Strip 'routinely'.

findings.claim: The financial-manager role is hedging; speculating is out of scope.
findings.failure_mode: Supported by the converted source but not carried in the deep ref; the source frames it as the chapter's perspective rather than a role boundary.
findings.evidence: Deep 734 (definitions only). Source 33137-33139: 'In this chapter, however, the focus is on the perspective of a financial manager using these strategies to manage risk.'
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to Ch 20.1 'Risk and Firm Value': 'Many of these same strategies can be used by economic players who wish to speculate' [V]; 'the focus is on the perspective of a financial manager using these strategies to manage risk' [V]. Then correct line 42 to: The chapter takes the financial manager's perspective of using these strategies to manage risk, not to speculate.

findings.claim: What's the breakeven volume? At list price, what is the contribution-margin NPV ...? (Ch 18.3; Ch 19.1) / contribution-margin and breakeven framing / CVP/breakeven framing carries through (Ch 16.2; Ch 18.5)

findings.fix: correct: cite breakeven and contribution margin to OpenStax Principles of Accounting Vol 2 (Ch 3); keep Ch 18.3 for variable costs as a percentage of sales.

findings.claim: What is the dilutive cost of stock-based compensation over the expected vesting horizon? ... (Ch 17.6, "Issuing New Common Stock") / equity dilution as financing cost (Ch 17.6)
findings.failure_mode: Ch 17.6 'Issuing New Common Stock' covers flotation costs and new equity as the most expensive capital; it does not treat stock-based compensation or its dilution. The source places stock-based compensation under agency mitigations (Ch 2.4).

findings.fix: correct: cite Ch 17.6 only for 'issuing new common stock is the most expensive form of capital'; label the SBC-dilution pricing as the distillation's extension.

findings.claim: on earnings (which can be manipulated) or on cash flow (which cannot)? / earnings can be manipulated through estimates; cash flows cannot.
findings.failure_mode: Hardens a comparative into an absolute. The source says cash flows are 'far less easily manipulated', not immune.
findings.evidence: Deep 419 (Ch 11.3) [V]: cash flows 'are far less easily manipulated through accounting treatments than revenues or bottom-line earnings'. Source 19142-19143.
findings.fix: correct: ... or on cash flow, which is 'far less easily manipulated through accounting treatments' [V] (Ch 11.3)?

findings.section: Worked Example, Setting the discount rate
findings.claim: consistent with the source's instruction to adjust CAPM-derived equity cost upward for project-specific risk
findings.failure_mode: The source says the project's discount rate 'can be increased or decreased' for project risk; it gives no instruction to adjust the CAPM equity cost.
findings.evidence: Source 26977-26979 (Ch 16.2): 'the discount rate used to discount future cash flows to the present can be increased or decreased to adjust for the riskiness of the project's cash flows.' Deep 565.
findings.fix: correct: consistent with the source's note that the discount rate 'can be increased or decreased to adjust for the riskiness of the project's cash flows' (Ch 16.2).

findings.claim: At 18 per cent discount rate, the NPV of the cash flow stream is approximately $1.1 million. IRR is approximately 32 per cent. / If the velocity improvement is 50 per cent of estimate ... NPV falls to approximately $0.1 million ... If velocity is 25 per cent of estimate, NPV becomes negative.
findings.failure_mode: Internal arithmetic error in the hypothetical, repeated in the board paper and both lens sections. The stated inputs ($1.8M upfront; $750k + $150k + $400k = $1.3M/yr; 5 years; 18 per cent) give NPV of about $1.8-2.3M and IRR of about 64-67 per cent; at 50 per cent velocity NPV is about $0.8-1.1M, and at 25 per cent it stays positive. The example's sensitivity story (marginal at half, negative at a quarter) does not follow from its own numbers.
findings.evidence: Recomputed: annual timing NPV $2,265,322, IRR 66.6%; monthly timing with 6-month build and 3-month ramp NPV $1,788,950, IRR 63.8%; half-velocity NPV $1,092,633 / $771,136; quarter-velocity NPV $506,289 / $262,229.
findings.fix: correct: either rescale the inputs (e.g. annual benefits near $0.9M) so the stated NPV, IRR and sensitivity thresholds hold, or restate the outputs from the given inputs (NPV ≈ $2.2M, IRR ≈ 65 per cent, still positive at 25 per cent of the velocity estimate) and update lines 154, 189, 191.

findings.claim: This follows the source's direction to run sensitivity analysis — "identify which inputs are load-bearing" — ... / The source's scenario-analysis method — "multiple inputs changing together, modelling recession / base / expansion" —
findings.failure_mode: Quote marks present the distillation's own Key Concept 11 wording as the source's; the concepts are supported, the words are not the source's.
findings.evidence: Deep 685 (Ch 18.5): sensitivity 'useful for identifying which forecast inputs are most consequential'; scenario = recession / normal / expansion. Neither quoted phrase appears in the source.
findings.fix: correct: drop the quotation marks and paraphrase with citation (Ch 18.5, "Sensitivity Analysis in Forecasting"; "Scenarios in Forecasting").

findings.claim: the source's expectation that forecasting produces learning priors, not one-time commitments. (Source: Ch 18.1)
findings.failure_mode: Loosened: the source contrasts a static budget with a rolling forecast that adjusts as new information arrives; 'learning priors' is the distillation's framing.
findings.evidence: Deep 659 (Ch 18.1): 'A budget is a static forecast; a rolling forecast adjusts as time passes and new information arrives.' Source 30265.
findings.fix: correct: the source's rolling forecast, which 'adjust[s] as time moves on' and new information arrives (Ch 18).

findings.claim: Accounting Vol 2 contributes the cost-classification, CVP, relevant-cost, and theory-of-constraints machinery for *operating* decisions; this reference contributes the capital-budgeting and capital-structure machinery for *investment and financing* decisions.
findings.failure_mode: The operating/investment split misdescribes Accounting Vol 2, which also covers capital budgeting (payback, ARR, NPV, IRR, PI) in Ch 11.
findings.evidence: openstax-accounting-vol2-deep 17 (short-term vs long-term frames), 299-330 (Ch 11 capital budgeting).
findings.fix: correct: Accounting Vol 2 contributes cost classification, CVP, relevant-cost and TOC machinery for operating decisions, plus an introductory capital-budgeting chapter (Ch 11: payback, ARR, NPV, IRR); this reference carries the fuller capital-budgeting, cost-of-capital and capital-structure machinery.
